title: Alexi Gladstone | Explorative Modeling -- Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation
excerpt: What in the world is Explorative Modeling?
content_html:
Website: https://explorative-modeling.github.io/ GitHub: https://github.com/alexiglad/XM

TLDR: We introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm for generative modeling that acts as a third pretraining axis when added to existing generative models, and also enables end-to-end generation. Increasing exploration monotonically improves existing models across images, video, and language, and the gains grow with scale (7%→36% with data, 13%→23% with parameters). Concretely, Explorative Models (XMs) reach 6.2× sample efficiency, 4.1× FLOP efficiency, and 47% better parameter efficiency. Exploration also enables scaling generalization, and scaling how end-to-end existing models are. As end-to-end generative models, XMs match diffusion on control tasks with up to 256× less inference compute.

Let me start with a question that sounds simple. If I ask a model to “generate a dog”, how many correct answers are there?

It turns out there are a lot… likely billions or more images that we could count as dog images.

So what happens if we train a neural network to directly predict dog images? The model sees thousands of different valid dogs during training, and the single prediction closest to all of them is their average. That’s what the model learns to output, and the average of thousands of dogs looks nothing like a dog, it’s a brown blur.

To make this concrete, let’s play a game. I’m going to throw darts at the board below, and each dart will land somewhere random on the rings. Your job is to guess where my next dart will land, and the further off you are, the worse your score.

So where should you guess? It turns out the guess that minimizes your error is the exact middle of the board.1 We trained a model to play this game, and sure enough, it guesses the middle every time (this is the optimal prediction here)!

This is terrible though… the middle is almost never where a dart actually lands. The “optimal” guess is a spot that no darts ever land.

This is the core problem of generative modeling. When a prediction has many valid answers, the best single prediction is their average, and the average of data is generally a bad answer that looks nothing like the real data.2

And this problem isn’t special to dartboards or dogs, it shows up with any kind of data. When we trained a model to directly generate three piles of 2D points, it predicted a single dot in the middle of them, and when we trained one on text, all it could say was “the”.

But wait. ChatGPT writes coherent text, and image models generate really amazing images. Clearly this problem has been solved somehow, right?

It has, and every scalable generative model today solves it the same way, by breaking generation into many small steps during training, so each step has roughly one right answer. When a step has one right answer, there’s nothing to average, and the blur disappears.

Let’s look at how this works. Autoregressive models (like LLMs) predict one piece at a time, which in our game means never guessing the dart’s exact position all at once. Instead, you first guess only how far left or right the dart lands, and then given that, you guess how far up or down. Once you know the dart landed on the far right, there are only a couple places it could be.

Diffusion models do this differently. They start from pure random noise and take hundreds of tiny steps toward the data. Early on, their guess could still become any dart, but every step narrows the possibilities, so no single step ever faces many valid answers at once.

It turns out this is basically how every modern generative model works, by breaking the generation process into smaller pieces that can be predicted well. This includes LLMs, image and video models, and even newer few-step models like MeanFlow and consistency models. We refer to this idea of breaking generation into pieces as factoring generation.

This approach of factoring generation works, but it’s also evil for a couple of reasons. The first is that models get trained on a single step, yet run for hundreds or thousands of steps at inference, so their own imperfect outputs get fed back in as inputs, errors compound, and generations slowly drift away from anything the model saw during training. This problem is called exposure bias (I wrote a whole blog on why it’s evil), and it’s why video models melt into mush after ten seconds and why LLMs get less coherent over really long generations, directly hurting performance and generalization.

The second evil builds on the first, because that mismatch between training and inference means these models are never end-to-end, where an end-to-end model runs at inference exactly the way it was trained. End-to-end learning is what kicked off the deep learning revolution with AlexNet, and the lesson has held ever since… letting models learn everything directly from data beats hand-designing parts of the pipeline, and a model that runs the way it was trained is never forced into out-of-distribution territory. Nearly all of deep learning has gone end-to-end by now except generative modeling, and factoring generation is exactly what’s blocking it.

So ideally we’d stop factoring generation, but factoring is also the only trick we know that handles the many-answers problem. The natural question then is whether we could factor something else instead, and it turns out a generative model only has two processes, how it generates and how it trains. If generation is off the table, that leaves the training loop.

So what does factoring training look like? To answer this, let’s go back to our game, except this time I’ll give you twenty guesses instead of one, and only your closest guess counts. It turns out that with twenty guesses, guessing the middle becomes a terrible strategy. This is because you can now spread your guesses over the spots where darts actually land, lowering your error far more than the middle ever could. In other words, the winning strategy is to use your guesses to explore different answers.

And this is exactly what happens. When we train a model this way with twenty guesses (middle panel below), its guesses spread across the board!

Take a second to appreciate what just happened here. The darts land in the exact same places as before, but because we changed how guesses are scored, the best possible prediction moved from the middle of the board onto the spots darts actually land. This reveals something important, which is that the training objective alone controls what the best prediction is (the loss minimizer), and by changing it, we moved the loss minimizer from the average of the data onto the data itself.

This is Explorative Modeling. At each training step, the model explores K possible matches between what it generates and the real data, and only the best match gets trained. We call models trained this way Explorative Models (XMs). In the simplest case, this is literally, beautifully, a for loop:

losses = []
for i in range(K):
    generation = model.generate()  # e.g., from a different random noise
    losses.append(loss_fn(generation, data))
min(losses).backward()  # only the best generation gets gradients

Here’s what happens as we increase the exploration K on real data:

If we zoom out, this figure actually hints at something much bigger. All of modern generative modeling is really about designing a training objective whose loss minimizer lands on real data instead of between it, and factoring generation and exploration are just two different ways of achieving this. We call this idea Mode Forcing, and it’s the theory that led us to Explorative Modeling in the first place, predicting almost every result in the paper before we ran the experiments. There’s a whole paper on Mode Forcing coming soon :)

Another thing worth noticing is that all of an XM’s extra work happens during training. For end-to-end XMs, generation itself is left completely untouched, staying a single step that works identically during training and inference.

So why does exploring more keep helping? It turns out that K controls how many distinct answers a model can commit to. With one guess, the model has to average everything, but with twenty, it can commit to twenty different answers that each specialize to a different part of the data. In the paper we call this capacity generative expressivity, the number of distinct answers a model can capture.

What’s crazy is that generative expressivity has been almost completely overlooked, to the point where the term didn’t even exist before this and the Mode Forcing paper.3 Yet it matters just as much as parameters and data. A model with a single parameter can’t do much no matter how much data you feed it, and in the exact same way, a model with a generative expressivity of one can’t do much no matter how many parameters and data you give it… its best possible output is still the blur (look at the K=1 column of Figure 8). For over a decade we’ve scaled parameters, which set what a model can represent, and data, which sets what a model can learn, while generative expressivity, what a model can generate, has stayed fixed, baked into the training objective. Factoring generation was the field’s fix for this, but the expressivity it supplies is frozen the moment you design the model, whereas exploration turns it into something you can actually scale. This is exactly why scaling generative expressivity through exploration is a third pretraining axis, and as we’ll see below, the empirical results back this up.

At this point we know what Explorative Modeling is, so how do we actually use it? Looking back at Figure 9, there are two ways, combining exploration with existing generative models, or using it as a standalone approach. Combining exploration with existing models is where the new pretraining axis comes from, whereas using XMs as a standalone approach is what enables end-to-end generation.

Let’s start with existing generative models. At first glance it might seem like they don’t need more generative expressivity, since factoring generation already handles the many-answers problem. But if you look closely, single steps inside diffusion or autoregression can still face many valid answers at once, meaning some blurring remains.4 Even worse, as models and datasets grow, parameters and data stop being the bottleneck while generative expressivity stays frozen, so we’d expect it to increasingly become the thing holding models back. If all of this is true, then adding exploration to existing models should improve them, with gains that grow with scale.

To test this, we added exploration on top of existing generative models while changing nothing else about their recipes, not even the hyperparameters.

We started with RAE, the ~state-of-the-art ImageNet generation recipe. Adding exploration reaches RAE’s final performance with 6.2× less data and 4.1× fewer FLOPs, and hits a ~state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet 256 without guidance. The speedups also compound across recipes, where XRAE converges 6.2× faster than RAE, which itself converges 47× faster than the standard SiT recipe, making XRAE almost 300× faster to converge than SiT.

The same story holds on an optimally tuned SiT baseline trained at a third of the compute, where exploration improves FLOP efficiency by up to 52% and reaches the same performance with 2.5× less data.

There’s also a subtle hint hiding in these plots, where the compute-optimal amount of exploration grows over the course of training (look at the crossovers in the FLOPs plots), directly mimicking how the compute-optimal number of parameters grows with compute in Chinchilla scaling. This reinforces that exploration really is a new pretraining axis, along with some more results below.

We also tested this on domains beyond images, adding exploration to video generation and masked diffusion language models while varying only the amount of exploration. In every domain, more exploration steadily improved performance, with some video models gaining over 20%, and the gains showed no sign of stopping at the largest K we tested.

The most important result, though, is that the gains from exploration grow with scale. As data scaled, gains rose from 7% to 36%. As models scaled, gains rose from 13% to 23%. And the efficiency gains above more than doubled when we tripled the compute. This is exactly what you’d expect if generative expressivity is a real third axis. Small models are held back by parameters and data, but as those scale, the fixed generative expressivity increasingly becomes the bottleneck, and exploration is what relieves it.

For reference, frontier training runs use roughly 10,000× more compute than our largest experiments. If these trends of gains growing with scale hold, the numbers here are probably a lower bound.

It turns out exploration improves generalization as well. To see why, remember that during pretraining the same input often gets paired with many different valid targets, which to a model that can only predict one thing looks like noise, and fitting noise is memorization. With exploration, each prediction instead trains toward the target it’s already closest to, so the targets become consistent and what looked like noise becomes structure the model can actually learn.5 We see this directly in our experiments, where models with more exploration overfit less on a fixed dataset and reach better performance (a best FVD of 30.0 vs 37.5 without exploration). In other words, extra training compute directly buys generalization, which I find especially exciting as data, not compute, increasingly becomes the bottleneck for large-scale training.

So exploration clearly works as a pretraining axis, but what about end-to-end generation? One of the biggest implications of generative expressivity is that factoring generation and exploration supply the exact same thing, which means they should be interchangeable. We demonstrate this directly below, where as exploration increases, the best-performing models use less and less generation factorization, meaning models that are more end-to-end benefit the most from exploration.

This makes how end-to-end your model is not a fixed design choice, but rather something you can scale. We can scale end-to-endedness :)

Taking this to its limit, we trained fully end-to-end XMs, where sampling is exactly the same at training and inference. On behavior cloning, our Explorative Policy matches Diffusion Policy with a single forward pass instead of 100:

Method Forward passes Lift Can Square Transport Tool Hang
Diffusion Policy 100 100% 100% 94% 72% 86%
Explorative Policy 1 100% 100% 96% 74% 86%

And our Explorative World Model matches Diffuser on goal-conditioned world modeling with 16-256× fewer forward passes:

Method Score (avg) Forward passes (avg)
Diffuser 127.2 192
Explorative World Model 130.0 2.3

The reason this is even possible comes back to what each approach factors, where diffusion pays for its generative expressivity with generation steps at inference, while XMs pay for it through exploration during training.

So where does this leave us? If you train robotics policies, world models, image, video, or audio generation models, masked diffusion language models, or really any generative model whose predictions face many valid answers (i.e., models working on decently multimodal distributions), you can add exploration with a for loop, without touching your architecture or hyperparameters (there’s pseudocode on the website if you want to try). In our experiments, adding exploration improved FLOP efficiency, data efficiency, parameter efficiency, and generalization across every domain we tried, so there’s a good chance it does the same for you! The best way to predict whether XMs will help is to determine how many valid answers each of your model’s predictions faces. The more answers per prediction, and the bigger your scale, the more exploration has to offer, while predictions with one clear answer (less multimodal) will likely benefit less (although benefits are still possible, as the paper discusses and lightly experiments with).

This rule of thumb also explains why autoregressive LLMs are the one place we’ve tested so far where exploration hasn’t been an immediate win, since predicting the next token given a long context is already close to having one right answer, and LLMs have no natural latent variable to explore over. That said, we’ve already seen modest early gains in data efficiency for autoregressive LLMs, and we have several ideas for pushing further, such as multi-token prediction, which faces far more valid answers per prediction, or conditioning on a learned latent, which would give exploration something to search over. I believe exploration will eventually make LLMs more end-to-end and better-scaling too, it just needs more work.

Longer term, the two directions I’m most excited about are Reverse XM and gradient-based exploration. Reverse XM flips the search so that one generation searches over K datapoints instead of one datapoint searching over K generations, which costs almost no extra compute and in principle lets K grow to the size of the entire dataset. Gradient-based exploration would replace random guessing with directly descending the loss to find the best latent. Pushed far enough, either one turns generative modeling into pure search for good latents with a very large K.

Taking a step back, the coolest part of this project to me is where it all came from. It didn’t start with tinkering or a lucky ablation, it started with deeply understanding why generative modeling is hard, which to me was an aha moment that resulted in all of Mode Forcing and ultimately ended up resulting in predicting all these results beforehand. And if you look back, that’s exactly the path this blog just walked… we started from first principles, arrived at Explorative Modeling as a way to increase generative expressivity, and from there got both a new pretraining axis and end-to-end generation.

If there was one takeaway from this paper, I’d say it’s the following:

We scale the size of generative models and how much data we train them on… so why haven’t we scaled what they can generate?

Huge thanks to my collaborators Yilun Du and Heng Ji, and to everyone who supported this work! Check out the paper and website for more details/depth!

  1. Being scored by squared distance means your best guess is the average of all landing spots, and for rings centered on the board, that average is the exact middle. ↩

  2. The formal name for this is a multimodal distribution, a distribution with many distinct peaks (called modes), where each mode is a valid answer. The paper talks about “capturing modes instead of averaging them”, which is this exact idea. ↩

  3. To be fair, people have long known that generative models need to capture modes instead of averaging them, and problems like mode collapse are well studied. What’s been missing is formalizing this as a capacity of the training objective itself, and recognizing just how central it is. Mode Forcing’s core claim is that having enough generative expressivity is the most important property of a generative training objective, and that even modern approaches like diffusion and autoregression have a fixed amount of it, a fundamental limit that scaling parameters and data can’t fix. ↩

  4. There’s fun indirect evidence for this. Classifier-free guidance, which nearly all image models rely on, improves samples by pushing them away from a blurrier version of the model. If models weren’t blurring at all, there would be nothing to push away from. ↩

In other words, extra training compute directly buys generalization, which I find especially exciting as data, not compute, increasingly becomes the bottleneck for large-scale training. Figure 14: More exploration overfits less on a fixed dataset, reaching better performance. So exploration clearly works as a pretraining axis, but what about end-to-end generation? One of the biggest implications of generative expressivity is that factoring generation and exploration supply the exact same thing, which means they should be interchangeable. We demonstrate this directly below, where as exploration increases, the best-performing models use less and less generation factorization, meaning models that are more end-to-end benefit the most from exploration. Figure 15: As exploration increases, the best models use fewer generation steps. This makes how end-to-end your model is not a fixed design choice, but rather something you can scale. We can scale end-to-endedness :) Taking this to its limit, we trained fully end-to-end XMs, where sampling is exactly the same at training and inference. On behavior cloning, our Explorative Policy matches Diffusion Policy with a single forward pass instead of 100: Method Forward passes Lift Can Square Transport Tool Hang Diffusion Policy 100 100% 100% 94% 72% 86% Explorative Policy 1 100% 100% 96% 74% 86% And our Explorative World Model matches Diffuser on goal-conditioned world modeling with 16-256× fewer forward passes: Method Score (avg) Forward passes (avg) Diffuser 127.2 192 Explorative World Model 130.0 2.3 The reason this is even possible comes back to what each approach factors, where diffusion pays for its generative expressivity with generation steps at inference, while XMs pay for it through exploration during training. So where does this leave us? If you train robotics policies, world models, image, video, or audio generation models, masked diffusion language models, or really any generative model whose predictions face many valid answers (i.e., models working on decently multimodal distributions), you can add exploration with a for loop, without touching your architecture or hyperparameters (there’s pseudocode on the website if you want to try). In our experiments, adding exploration improved FLOP efficiency, data efficiency, parameter efficiency, and generalization across every domain we tried, so there’s a good chance it does the same for you! The best way to predict whether XMs will help is to determine how many valid answers each of your model’s predictions faces. The more answers per prediction, and the bigger your scale, the more exploration has to offer, while predictions with one clear answer (less multimodal) will likely benefit less (although benefits are still possible, as the paper discusses and lightly experiments with). This rule of thumb also explains why autoregressive LLMs are the one place we’ve tested so far where exploration hasn’t been an immediate win, since predicting the next token given a long context is already close to having one right answer, and LLMs have no natural latent variable to explore over. That said, we’ve already seen modest early gains in data efficiency for autoregressive LLMs, and we have several ideas for pushing further, such as multi-token prediction, which faces far more valid answers per prediction, or conditioning on a learned latent, which would give exploration something to search over. I believe exploration will eventually make LLMs more end-to-end and better-scaling too, it just needs more work. Longer term, the two directions I’m most excited about are Reverse XM and gradient-based exploration. Reverse XM flips the search so that one generation searches over K datapoints instead of one datapoint searching over K generations, which costs almost no extra compute and in principle lets K grow to the size of the entire dataset. Gradient-based exploration would replace random guessing with directly descending the loss to find the best latent. Pushed far enough, either one turns generative modeling into pure search for good latents with a very large K. Taking a step back, the coolest part of this project to me is where it all came from. It didn’t start with tinkering or a lucky ablation, it started with deeply understanding why generative modeling is hard, which to me was an aha moment that resulted in all of Mode Forcing and ultimately ended up resulting in predicting all these results beforehand. And if you look back, that’s exactly the path this blog just walked… we started from first principles, arrived at Explorative Modeling as a way to increase generative expressivity, and from there got both a new pretraining axis and end-to-end generation. If there was one takeaway from this paper, I’d say it’s the following: We scale the size of generative models and how much data we train them on… so why haven’t we scaled what they can generate? Huge thanks to my collaborators Yilun Du and Heng Ji, and to everyone who supported this work! Check out the paper and website for more details/depth! blocks.html_en: This approach of factoring generation works, but it’s also evil for a couple of reasons. The first is that models get trained on a single step, yet run for hundreds or thousands of steps at inference, so their own imperfect outputs get fed back in as inputs, errors compound, and generations slowly drift away from anything the model saw during training. This problem is called exposure bias (I wrote a whole blog on why it’s evil), and it’s why video models melt into mush after ten seconds and why LLMs get less coherent over really long generations, directly hurting performance and generalization.

blocks.html_en: The second evil builds on the first, because that mismatch between training and inference means these models are never end-to-end, where an end-to-end model runs at inference exactly the way it was trained. blocks.html_en: So what does factoring training look like? To answer this, let’s go back to our game, except this time I’ll give you twenty guesses instead of one, and only your closest guess counts. It turns out that with twenty guesses, guessing the middle becomes a terrible strategy. This is because you can now spread your guesses over the spots where darts actually land, lowering your error far more than the middle ever could. In other words, the winning strategy is to use your guesses to explore different answers.

blocks.html_en: So why does exploring more keep helping? It turns out that K controls how many distinct answers a model can commit to. With one guess, the model has to average everything, but with twenty, it can commit to twenty different answers that each specialize to a different part of the data. In the paper we call this capacity generative expressivity, the number of distinct answers a model can capture.

sentences.zh: 如果有一个猜测，模型必须对所有内容进行平均，但是如果有 20 个猜测，它就可以得出 20 个不同的答案，每个答案专门针对数据的不同部分。

sentences.en: In the paper we call this capacity generative expressivity, the number of distinct answers a model can capture.
sentences.zh: 在本文中，我们将这种能力称为生成表达能力，即模型可以捕获的不同答案的数量。

blocks.html_en: What’s crazy is that generative expressivity has been almost completely overlooked, to the point where the term didn’t even exist before this and the Mode Forcing paper.3 Yet it matters just as much as parameters and data. A model with a single parameter can’t do much no matter how much data you feed it, and in the exact same way, a model with a generative expressivity of one can’t do much no matter how many parameters and data you give it… its best possible output is still the blur (look at the K=1 column of Figure 8). For over a decade we’ve scaled parameters, which set what a model can represent, and data, which sets what a model can learn, while generative expressivity, what a model can generate, has stayed fixed, baked into the training objective. Factoring generation was the field’s fix for this, but the expressivity it supplies is frozen the moment you design the model, whereas exploration turns it into something you can actually scale. This is exactly why scaling generative expressivity through exploration is a third pretraining axis, and as we’ll see below, the empirical results back this up.

blocks.html_en: At this point we know what Explorative Modeling is, so how do we actually use it? Looking back at Figure 9, there are two ways, combining exploration with existing generative models, or using it as a standalone approach. Combining exploration with existing models is where the new pretraining axis comes from, whereas using XMs as a standalone approach is what enables end-to-end generation.

blocks.html_en: Let’s start with existing generative models. At first glance it might seem like they don’t need more generative expressivity, since factoring generation already handles the many-answers problem. But if you look closely, single steps inside diffusion or autoregression can still face many valid answers at once, meaning some blurring remains.4 Even worse, as models and datasets grow, parameters and data stop being the bottleneck while generative expressivity stays frozen, so we’d expect it to increasingly become the thing holding models back. If all of this is true, then adding exploration to existing models should improve them, with gains that grow with scale.

blocks.html_en: We started with RAE, the ~state-of-the-art ImageNet generation recipe. Adding exploration reaches RAE’s final performance with 6.2× less data and 4.1× fewer FLOPs, and hits a ~state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet 256 without guidance. The speedups also compound across recipes, where XRAE converges 6.2× faster than RAE, which itself converges 47× faster than the standard SiT recipe, making XRAE almost 300× faster to converge than SiT.

blocks.html_en: The most important result, though, is that the gains from exploration grow with scale. As data scaled, gains rose from 7% to 36%. As models scaled, gains rose from 13% to 23%. And the efficiency gains above more than doubled when we tripled the compute. This is exactly what you’d expect if generative expressivity is a real third axis. Small models are held back by parameters and data, but as those scale, the fixed generative expressivity increasingly becomes the bottleneck, and exploration is what relieves it.

blocks.html_en: It turns out exploration improves generalization as well. To see why, remember that during pretraining the same input often gets paired with many different valid targets, which to a model that can only predict one thing looks like noise, and fitting noise is memorization. With exploration, each prediction instead trains toward the target it’s already closest to, so the targets become consistent and what looked like noise becomes structure the model can actually learn.5 We see this directly in our experiments, where models with more exploration overfit less on a fixed dataset and reach better performance (a best FVD of 30.0 vs 37.5 without exploration). In other words, extra training compute directly buys generalization, which I find especially exciting as data, not compute, increasingly becomes the bottleneck for large-scale training.

blocks.html_en: So where does this leave us? If you train robotics policies, world models, image, video, or audio generation models, masked diffusion language models, or really any generative model whose predictions face many valid answers (i.e., models working on decently multimodal distributions), you can add exploration with a for loop, without touching your architecture or hyperparameters (there’s pseudocode on the website if you want to try). In our experiments, adding exploration improved FLOP efficiency, data efficiency, parameter efficiency, and generalization across every domain we tried, so there’s a good chance it does the same for you! The best way to predict whether XMs will help is to determine how many valid answers each of your model’s predictions faces. The more answers per prediction, and the bigger your scale, the more exploration has to offer, while predictions with one clear answer (less multimodal) will likely benefit less (although benefits are still possible, as the paper discusses and lightly experiments with).

blocks.html_en: Longer term, the two directions I’m most excited about are Reverse XM and gradient-based exploration. Reverse XM flips the search so that one generation searches over K datapoints instead of one datapoint searching over K generations, which costs almost no extra compute and in principle lets K grow to the size of the entire dataset. Gradient-based exploration would replace random guessing with directly descending the loss to find the best latent. Pushed far enough, either one turns generative modeling into pure search for good latents with a very large K.

网站：https://explorative-modeling.github.io/ GitHub：https://github.com/alexiglad/XM

TLDR：我们引入了探索性建模，这是一种生成建模的新范式，当添加到现有生成模型时，它可以充当第三个预训练轴，并且还可以实现端到端生成。 增加探索可以单调改善图像、视频和语言方面的现有模型，并且收益随着规模的扩大而增长（数据为 7%→36%，参数为 13%→23%）。 具体来说，探索性模型 (XM) 达到了 6.2 倍的样本效率、4.1 倍的 FLOP 效率和 47% 的参数效率。 探索还可以扩展泛化，并扩展现有模型的端到端程度。 作为端到端生成模型，XM 在控制任务上匹配扩散，推理计算量减少了 256 倍。

让我从一个听起来很简单的问题开始。 如果我要求模型“生成一只狗”，有多少个正确答案？

事实证明有很多…… 可能有数十亿或更多的图像可以算作狗图像。

那么如果我们训练一个神经网络来直接预测狗的图像会发生什么呢？ 该模型在训练过程中看到了数千只不同的有效狗，最接近所有狗的单个预测是它们的平均值。 这就是模型学习输出的内容，数千只狗的平均看起来一点也不像狗，而是棕色的模糊。

为了具体说明这一点，让我们玩一个游戏。 我将向下面的木板投掷飞镖，每个飞镖都会随机落在环上的某个位置。 你的任务是猜测我的下一个飞镖会落在哪里，距离越远，你的分数就越差。

那么你应该猜到哪里呢？ 事实证明，最小化错误的猜测就是棋盘的正中间。1 我们训练了一个模型来玩这个游戏，果然，它每次都猜测到中间（这是这里的最佳预测）！

虽然这很可怕…… 中间几乎不是飞镖真正落地的地方。 “最佳”猜测是没有飞镖落到的地方。

这是生成建模的核心问题。 当预测有许多有效答案时，最好的单个预测是它们的平均值，而数据的平均值通常是一个糟糕的答案，看起来与真实数据完全不同。2

这个问题对于飞镖或狗来说并不是特有的，它会出现在任何类型的数据中。 当我们训练一个模型直接生成三堆二维点时，它预测它们中间有一个点，而当我们在文本上训练一个模型时，它只能说“the”。

但等等。 ChatGPT 编写连贯的文本，图像模型生成真正令人惊叹的图像。 显然这个问题已经以某种方式解决了，对吧？

它已经做到了，并且当今每个可扩展的生成模型都以相同的方式解决这个问题，即在训练过程中将生成分解为许多小步骤，因此每个步骤大致都有一个正确答案。 当一个步骤有一个正确答案时，就没有什么可平均的，模糊就会消失。

让我们看看这是如何工作的。 自回归模型（如法学硕士）一次预测一件，这在我们的游戏中意味着永远不会一次性猜测飞镖的确切位置。 相反，你首先猜测飞镖落在左或右的距离，然后再猜测向上或向下的距离。 一旦你知道飞镖落在最右边，它就只有几个地方可能。

扩散模型的做法有所不同。 他们从纯随机噪声开始，对数据采取数百个微小步骤。 早期，他们的猜测仍然可能成为任何飞镖，但每一步都会缩小可能性，因此没有一个步骤会同时面临许多有效的答案。

事实证明，这基本上就是每个现代生成模型的工作原理，将生成过程分解成可以很好预测的更小的部分。 这包括法学硕士、图像和视频模型，甚至是更新的几步模型，如 MeanFlow 和一致性模型。 我们将这种将生成分解为多个部分的想法称为分解生成。

这种分解生成的方法是有效的，但由于几个原因它也是邪恶的。 首先，模型在​​单个步骤上进行训练，但在推理时运行数百或数千个步骤，因此它们自己的不完美输出会随着输入、错误复合而反馈回来，并且世代会慢慢偏离模型在训练期间看到的任何内容。 这个问题被称为曝光偏差（我写了一篇完整的博客来解释为什么它是邪恶的），这就是为什么视频模型在十秒后就会融化成糊状，也是为什么法学硕士在很长的一代中变得不那么连贯，直接损害了性能和泛化能力。

第二个弊端建立在第一个弊端的基础上，因为训练和推理之间的不匹配意味着这些模型永远不是端到端的，而端到端模型在推理时的运行方式与训练时完全相同。 端到端学习开启了 AlexNet 的深度学习革命，从那时起，这个教训就一直存在…… 让模型直接从数据中学习一切，胜过手工设计流程的各个部分，并且按照训练方式运行的模型永远不会被迫进入分布范围之外。 到目前为止，除了生成建模之外，几乎所有深度学习都已实现端到端，而因子生成正是阻碍它的因素。

因此，理想情况下我们应该停止因式分解生成，但因式分解也是我们所知道的处理多答案问题的唯一技巧。 那么自然的问题是我们是否可以考虑其他因素，事实证明生成模型只有两个过程，即如何生成和如何训练。 如果生成不可行，那就离开训练循环。

那么保理培训是什么样的呢？ 为了回答这个问题，让我们回到我们的游戏，只不过这次我会给你二十个猜测而不是一个，而且只有你最接近的猜测才算数。 事实证明，有二十个猜测，猜测中间就变成了一个糟糕的策略。 这是因为您现在可以将您的猜测分散到飞镖实际落地的位置，从而比中间的位置更能降低您的错误。 换句话说，获胜的策略是利用你的猜测来探索不同的答案。

而这正是发生的事情。 当我们用二十个猜测（下面的中图）以这种方式训练模型时，它的猜测遍布整个棋盘！

花点时间来欣赏一下这里刚刚发生的事情。 飞镖落在与以前完全相同的位置，但由于我们改变了猜测的评分方式，因此最佳预测从棋盘中间转移到了飞镖实际落地的位置。 这揭示了一些重要的事情，即训练目标单独控制最佳预测是什么（损失最小化器），并且通过改变它，我们将损失最小化器从数据的平均值转移到数据本身。

这就是探索性建模。 在每个训练步骤中，模型都会探索其生成的数据与真实数据之间的 K 个可能匹配，并且仅对最佳匹配进行训练。 我们将这种方式训练的模型称为探索性模型 (XM)。 在最简单的情况下，这实际上是一个漂亮的 for 循环：

losses = []
for i in range(K):
    generation = model.generate()  # e.g., from a different random noise
    losses.append(loss_fn(generation, data))
min(losses).backward()  # only the best generation gets gradients

当我们增加对真实数据的探索 K 时，会发生以下情况：

如果我们缩小，这个数字实际上暗示着更大的事情。 所有现代生成模型实际上都是设计一个训练目标，其损失最小化器落在真实数据上而不是真实数据之间，而分解生成和探索只是实现这一目标的两种不同方式。 我们将这个想法称为“模式强制”，正是这个理论首先引导我们进行探索性建模，在我们进行实验之前预测了论文中的几乎所有结果。 即将推出关于模式强制的完整论文:)

另一件值得注意的事情是 XM 的所有额外工作都发生在训练期间。 对于端到端 XM，生成本身完全保持不变，在训练和推理过程中保持相同工作的单个步骤。

那么为什么探索更多仍然有帮助呢？ 事实证明，K 控制模型可以提交多少个不同的答案。 如果有一个猜测，模型必须对所有内容进行平均，但是如果有 20 个猜测，它就可以得出 20 个不同的答案，每个答案专门针对数据的不同部分。 在本文中，我们将这种能力称为生成表达能力，即模型可以捕获的不同答案的数量。

疯狂的是，生成表达性几乎完全被忽视了，以至于在这篇文章和《模式强制》论文之前，这个术语甚至不存在。3然而，它与参数和数据一样重要。 无论你提供多少数据，具有单个参数的模型都无法做太多事情，同样，无论你给它多少参数和数据，生成表达能力为 1 的模型也无法做太多事情...... 它的最佳输出仍然是模糊（参见图 8 的 K=1 列）。 十多年来，我们缩放了参数（设置模型可以表示的内容）和数据（设置模型可以学习的内容），而生成表达性（模型可以生成的内容）保持固定，融入训练目标。 因式分解生成是该领域的解决方案，但它提供的表现力在您设计模型的那一刻就被冻结了，而探索将其变成了您可以实际扩展的东西。 这正是为什么通过探索来扩展生成表达能力是第三个预训练轴，正如我们将在下面看到的，实证结果支持了这一点。

至此我们知道了什么是探索性建模，那么我们如何实际使用它呢？ 回顾图 9，有两种方法，将探索与现有生成模型相结合，或将其用作独立方法。 将探索与现有模型相结合是新的预训练轴的来源，而使用 XM 作为独立方法则可以实现端到端生成。

让我们从现有的生成模型开始。 乍一看，他们似乎不需要更多的生成表达能力，因为因式分解生成已经处理了多答案问题。 但如果你仔细观察，扩散或自回归中的单个步骤仍然可以同时面临许多有效答案，这意味着仍然存在一些模糊。4更糟糕的是，随着模型和数据集的增长，参数和数据不再成为瓶颈，而生成表达能力保持冻结状态，因此我们预计它会越来越成为阻碍模型的因素。 如果所有这些都是真的，那么对现有模型进行探索应该会改进它们，收益会随着规模的扩大而增长。

为了测试这一点，我们在现有的生成模型之上添加了探索，同时不改变其配方的任何其他内容，甚至不改变超参数。

我们从 RAE 开始，这是最先进的 ImageNet 生成方法。 添加探索后，RAE 的最终性能减少了 6.2 倍的数据和 4.1 倍的 FLOP，并且在没有指导的情况下在 ImageNet 256 上达到了最先进的 1.43 FID。 不同配方之间的加速效果也是复合的，其中 XRAE 的收敛速度比 RAE 快 6.2 倍，RAE 本身的收敛速度比标准 SiT 配方快 47 倍，使得 XRAE 的收敛速度比 SiT 快近 300 倍。

同样的情况也适用于在三分之一的计算量上训练的经过优化调整的 SiT 基线，其中探索将 FLOP 效率提高了 52%，并在数据量减少 2.5 倍的情况下达到了相同的性能。

这些图中还隐藏着一个微妙的提示，其中计算最优的探索量在训练过程中不断增长（查看 FLOPs 图中的交叉），直接模仿计算最优参数数量如何随着 Chinchilla 缩放中的计算而增长。 这强化了探索确实是一个新的预训练轴，以及下面的更多结果。

我们还在图像以外的领域进行了测试，增加了对视频生成和掩蔽扩散语言模型的探索，同时仅改变探索的数量。 在每个领域，更多的探索稳步提高了性能，一些视频模型的性能提升超过 20%，而且在我们测试的最大 K 处，这种提升没有任何停止的迹象。

不过，最重要的结果是，勘探的收益随着规模的扩大而增长。 随着数据规模扩大，收益从 7% 上升至 36%。 随着模型规模的扩大，收益从 13% 上升到 23%。 当我们将计算量增加两倍时，效率提高了一倍以上。 如果生成表达力是真正的第三轴，这正是您所期望的。 小模型受到参数和数据的阻碍，但随着规模的扩大，固定的生成表达能力日益成为瓶颈，探索可以缓解这一瓶颈。

作为参考，前沿训练运行使用的计算量比我们最大的实验多大约 10,000 倍。 如果这些收益随规模增长的趋势持续存在，那么这里的数字可能是一个下限。

事实证明，探索也提高了泛化能力。 要了解原因，请记住，在预训练期间，相同的输入通常会与许多不同的有效目标配对，这对于只能预测一件事的模型来说看起来像是噪声，而拟合噪声就是记忆。 通过探索，每个预测都会朝着它已经最接近的目标进行训练，因此目标变得一致，看起来像噪声的东西变成了模型实际上可以学习的结构。5我们在实验中直接看到了这一点，其中具有更多探索的模型在固定数据集上的过度拟合更少，并达到更好的性能（最佳 FVD 为 30.0 与没有探索的 37.5）。 换句话说，额外的训练计算直接购买了泛化能力，我发现这特别令人兴奋，因为数据（而不是计算）日益成为大规模训练的瓶颈。

因此，探索显然可以作为预训练轴，但端到端生成又如何呢？ 生成表达性的最大含义之一是分解生成和探索提供完全相同的东西，这意味着它们应该是可以互换的。 我们在下面直接演示了这一点，随着探索的增加，性能最好的模型使用越来越少的生成分解，这意味着更加端到端的模型从探索中受益最多。

这使得端到端模型不再是固定的设计选择，而是可以扩展的。 我们可以扩展端到端的能力:)

考虑到这一点，我们训练了完全端到端的 XM，其中训练和推理时的采样完全相同。 在行为克隆方面，我们的探索性策略通过一次前向传播（而不是 100 次）与扩散策略相匹配：

这甚至是可能的原因可以追溯到每种方法所考虑的因素，其中扩散通过推理时的生成步骤为其生成表达性付出代价，而 XM 通过训练期间的探索为其付出代价。

那么这会给我们带来什么影响呢？ 如果您训练机器人策略、世界模型、图像、视频或音频生成模型、掩码扩散语言模型，或者任何其预测面临许多有效答案的生成模型（即，在适当的多模态分布上工作的模型），您可以使用 for 循环添加探索，而无需触及您的架构或超参数（如果您想尝试，网站上有伪代码）。 在我们的实验中，添加探索提高了我们尝试的每个领域的 FLOP 效率、数据效率、参数效率和泛化能力，因此很有可能它对您也有同样的作用！ 预测 XM 是否有帮助的最佳方法是确定每个模型的预测面临多少个有效答案。 每个预测的答案越多，规模越大，必须提供的探索就越多，而具有一个明确答案（较少多模态）的预测可能受益较少（尽管好处仍然是可能的，正如本文讨论和轻微实验的那样）。

这一经验法则也解释了为什么自回归法学硕士是我们迄今为止测试过的一个探索并未立即获胜的地方，因为在给定长上下文的情况下预测下一个标记已经接近于得到一个正确答案，并且法学硕士没有自然的潜在变量可供探索。 也就是说，我们已经看到自回归 LLM 的数据效率在早期取得了一定的进步，并且我们有一些进一步推进的想法，例如多标记预测，每个预测都面临更有效的答案，或者对学习的潜在变量进行调节，这将为探索提供一些可搜索的内容。 我相信探索最终将使法学硕士更加端到端和更好的扩展性，只是需要更多的工作。

从长远来看，我最兴奋的两个方向是 Reverse XM 和基于梯度的探索。 反向 XM 翻转搜索，使得一代搜索 K 个数据点，而不是一个数据点搜索 K 代，这几乎不需要额外的计算，原则上可以让 K 增长到整个数据集的大小。 基于梯度的探索将取代随机猜测，直接降低损失以找到最佳潜在变量。 如果推得足够远，任何一个都可以将生成模型转变为纯粹搜索具有非常大的 K 的良好潜在变量。

退一步来说，这个项目对我来说最酷的部分就是它的来源。 它并不是从修补或幸运的消融开始，而是从深刻理解为什么生成建模很难开始，这对我来说是一个顿悟时刻，它导致了所有模式强制，并最终导致提前预测所有这些结果。 如果你回头看，这正是这个博客刚刚走过的路…… 我们从第一原理开始，将探索性建模作为提高生成表达能力的一种方式，并从那里得到了新的预训练轴和端到端生成。

如果这篇论文有一个要点的话，我想说的是：

我们缩放生成模型的大小以及训练它们的数据量...... 那么我们为什么不扩大它们所能产生的规模呢？
